newsitem.title: USA: NYS Speaker rejects Gov budget,Senate on offensive.
newsitem.headline: NYS Speaker rejects Gov budget,Senate on offensive.

text.p: New York State's budget battle turned ugly on Wednesday, only a day after Gov George Pataki unveiled his proposals, as the Assembly rejected much of his plan and the Senate said the other house was holding up work.

Pataki has said his $66.1 billion budget for fiscal 1998 advances his effort to make the state more competitive by cutting estate and property taxes and slashing Medicaid, while increasing funds for new prisons and education.

Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver (D-Manhattan) left the door open to reducing property taxes but assailed the governor's proposal on this issue, as well as the proposal to cut Medicaid by $572 million. He also disputed Pataki's claim that his budget would raise aid for schools, and suggested the governor probably was underestimating revenues.

Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno (R-Troy) accused Silver of stopping the work of the bipartisan Bill Drafting Commission as a way of forcing the governor to approve $56,000 of stipends for seven Assembly members.

Pataki rejected the stipends at a special session late last year, according to Bruno, because the Speaker failed to approve bills as agreed, including a $12 billion capital program for the Metropolitan Transportation Agency and an energy bill for ratepayers.
A spokeswoman for the Republican governor had no comment immediately available.
Much of Silver's criticism centered on what he said was Pataki's favoring of some upstate voters and failing to aid the middleclass.

"It's unfair to the middle class, the budget is unfair to upstate, it's unfair to downstate," he told reporters in Albany. Estimating Pataki's property tax cut would save Westchester County residents 2-1/2 times the statewide average, though Erie County would see little benefit, he added: "As it stands right now, it is a budget that is unacceptable to us."

The Speaker said he would support an across-the-board cut in property taxes, but criticized the governor's plan, saying his five-year program would take too long. Pataki proposed a $3.4 billion plan to cut school property taxes by an average of 27 percent over four years and give schools more money.

Further, Silver said that according to his staff's calculations, which assume the state's schools need $1 billion in fiscal 1998, the governor's plan would leave them short $832 million, a gap districts would have to fill by raising property taxes.
Pataki has said that balancing the budget depends on slashing Medicaid, the joint state and federal program for the poor.

But his Democratic opponent, calling the cuts "the cruelest side" of the budget, forecast that it would cost health care providers $2.8 billion and cause 28,000 workers to lose their jobs. The governor has pointed to the greater use of managed care and the strong profits produced by hospitals in 1996 to justify the cutbacks.
And Silver signalled that the Assembly was fully prepared not only to fight some of the governor's budget cuts, including a tuition hike for state universities, but to raise spending as it saw fit.
"I believe the governor is underestimating revenues," he said, adding that he expected this would be the third year in a row that had happened.
The Pataki Administration has said it expects to end fiscal 1997 on March 31 with a surplus of about $1.3 billion, which will help trim a 1998 budget gap projected to be about $2.3 billion.

New York State last year set a new, national record for tardiness when it failed to approve until July its budget, due on April 1, and the Senate Leader, who has threatened to let expire rent rules that mainly affect New York City residents, Silver's home base, gave a graphic description of the kind of roadblocks that already have developed.
He accused Silver of holding up the payroll for the 200 staffers on the bill drafting commission in the battle over stipends, which are called lulus.
"The speaker takes the position that because the lulus didn't happen, nothing else is going to happen," Bruno told reporters in Albany.
